50284583.headline: Ty Jerome scores 31 points to lead the Grizzlies to a 123-112 win over the Kings
paras: SACRAMENTO, Calif. -- — Ty Jerome had 31 points, making all 14 of his free throw attempts, to lead the Memphis Grizzlies to a 123-112 win over the Sacramento Kings on Sunday night.

Jerome, coming off a 45-point performance in Memphis’ season opener, is leading the NBA in scoring at 36.5 points per game. He was limited to 15 games for the Grizzlies last season because of injuries.
Rookie Cameron Boozer contributed 16 points and 11 rebounds, and Cedric Coward had 15 points and 11 rebounds for the Grizzlies, who opened the season 3-0. Jaylen Wells had 16 points.
Zach LaVine had 37 points and five assists to lead the Kings, and rookie Darius Acuff Jr. had 22 points on 9 of 23 shots from the field. Domantas Sabonis had 15 points and 15 rebounds.
The Grizzlies built a 54-44 lead on back-to-back triples by Cam Spencer in the second quarter. Memphis led by 11 points in the second quarter and finished the first half with a 67-59 lead.
Memphis made 7 of 14 shots beyond the arc in the second quarter and outscored Sacramento 42-31, with seven players making at least one 3-pointer in the first half.

The Kings fought back to tie the game 106-106 on a three-point play by Sabonis at the 5:41 mark of the final quarter. The Grizzlies responded with a three-point play by Isaiah Stewart, a basket by Coward, and a 3-pointer by Jerome to move up by eight points.
Zach Edey missed the game due to left ankle injury management for the Grizzlies, and Keegan Murray was sidelined with an illness.
Up next Grizzlies: At Utah on Monday night.
Kings: At San Antonio on Tuesday night.

50287191.headline: Jalen Williams, Cason Wallace injured: What's next for the OKC Thunder?
paras: The Oklahoma City Thunder lost two starters to long-term injuries in their 108-101 win over the LA Clippers on Sunday night.

General manager Sam Presti announced Monday that guard Jalen Williams will undergo surgery for a dislocated left ankle and fractured fibula, while guard Cason Wallace will undergo surgery for a torn labrum in his left shoulder. Both players are expected to miss several months.
Williams was placed on a stretcher and wheeled off the court after he was injured on a drive to the basket late in the fourth quarter. Wallace left the game in the first quarter and didn't return.

They're both big losses for the Thunder, who were counting on Williams to get back to his All-Star form from the 2024-25 season and Wallace to step into the starting lineup. Williams missed 49 regular-season games last season while recovering from surgery on his right wrist and then injuring both hamstrings. He played in just five games -- and 107 total minutes -- in the postseason as OKC was beaten by the San Antonio Spurs in seven games in the Western Conference finals. Wallace signed a five-year, $139 million contract extension just before the season began.

How bad do these injuries hurt the Thunder, who are 3-0 and believe they have the talent to make it back to the NBA Finals? Do they have flexibility to make a move to replace Williams or Wallace? ESPN's reporters and analysts weigh in:
What was the early word on Williams' injury inside the Thunder? Emotional devastation, as evidenced by Shai Gilgeous-Alexander tearing up on the court.

It's gut-wrenching any time a player suffers a gruesome injury, but hearts are especially heavy for Williams in Oklahoma City. This is a young star who has had horrific injury luck despite doing everything right in terms of conditioning and rehab.

Williams' performance during the 2025 title run -- toughing it out with a shooting wrist that required surgery and still delivering 40 points in pivotal Game 5 of the NBA Finals -- will always be legendary in Oklahoma City. His injury misfortune has been miserable since with recurring hamstring strains that robbed him of most of last season and this cruel twist a week into this season.

The Thunder are a tight-knit team that has had to deal with the emotional consequences that come with the business of basketball. It stung to see title-winning teammates Luguentz Dort, Isaiah Joe and Aaron Wiggins traded in salary-slashing deals. This injury causes a deeper pain that the Thunder will have to process while figuring out how to fill a massive hole in the lineup. -- Tim MacMahon

How big of a hole will these losses leave for Oklahoma City? These two injuries are the most important development of the new season's first week in terms of how they change the championship picture. The Thunder still have excellent depth and star power at the guard and center positions, but they already shed a fair amount of perimeter depth over the summer by trading Dort, Wiggins and Joe. Without Williams in particular, they're now perilously thin on the wing.

Williams' absence hurts the Thunder on offense -- his unavailability might well have prevented the Thunder from scoring enough to beat the Spurs in the playoffs last season -- but at least they still have Ajay Mitchell and Jared McCain supporting two-time MVP Gilgeous-Alexander on that end. The larger problem comes on defense, which is the core of the Thunder's identity. They've led the league in defensive rating in each of the past two seasons and rank second thus far in 2026-27.

Last season, the Thunder had four perimeter players who were recent All-Defensive honorees. Trading Dort removed one of them, and the injuries to Williams and Wallace remove two more. For now, that series of unfortunate events leaves only Alex Caruso among the Thunder's elite perimeter defenders, and Oklahoma City prefers to load-manage him throughout the season to keep him fresh for the postseason. (Caruso has averaged 18.8 minutes per game in the regular season with the Thunder, versus 24.1 in the playoffs.)

Even if Wallace can return from his torn labrum for the postseason, he's smaller and less physically stout than either Dort or Williams, which could create significant problems as the Thunder contend with the other top teams in the West. In the postseason, they'll need to defend some combination of De'Aaron Fox, Dylan Harper and Stephon Castle; LaMelo Ball and Anthony Edwards; Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves; and Amen Thompson and Kevin Durant. Caruso can't guard them all.

Moreover, the simultaneous injuries to Williams and Wallace further eat away at Oklahoma City's margin of error, which had been meaningfully reduced by the team's summer trades. The new season is just three games old, and more injuries are probably coming -- but the Thunder can't afford to suffer more because their roster depth isn't as strong as it was a year or two ago. -- Zach Kram

How much flexibility do the Thunder have to make a move? Oklahoma City will likely receive a $15 million disabled player exception. The exception would allow the team to sign or trade for a player in the last year of his contract. Using more than $6.9 million, however, would cause the Thunder to exceed the second apron. They are not hard-capped and can go past the threshold.

Besides the potential disabled player exception, Oklahoma City also has three large trade exceptions: $17.8 million, $11.3 million and $9.2 million. The Thunder are allowed to use the trade exception and still exceed the second apron.
The McCain trade last season showed their willingness to add to their roster during the regular season.
Oklahoma City has seven tradeable first-round picks -- including three in the 2027 draft -- and 21 second-rounders available. -- Bobby Marks

Are there any natural targets available for OKC to pursue? As Bobby notes, Oklahoma City's financial situation will make it difficult to trade for another high-salary contributor. The only Thunder players making more than $7.8 million this season are effectively untradeable: Williams, Gilgeous-Alexander, Caruso, Chet Holmgren and Isaiah Hartenstein.

Barring a shocking trade of one of those players -- a swap involving Williams is perhaps feasible in a vacuum if the Thunder want to maximize their championship chances this season, but it seems inconceivable in context -- the Thunder won't be able to match the salaries of potential targets such as Trey Murphy III (New Orleans) or Michael Porter Jr. (Brooklyn). Nor will they be able to replace Williams' rare combination of offense, defense and size.

A handful of flawed, lower-cost trade targets from teams seemingly bound for the lottery would be more attainable, however. Murphy's teammate Herb Jones is a much lesser offensive player but could replace Williams' defensive impact; he also might be on the way out in New Orleans, as new Pelicans coach Jamahl Mosley has removed him from the starting lineup and slashed his playing time. The Wizards' Justin Champagnie is enjoying a strong start to the season and would add a brotherly element to the Thunder's rivalry with the Spurs and Julian Champagnie.

From Golden State, De'Anthony Melton and Gary Payton II will be eligible to be traded after Dec. 15 and would fill a Wallace-sized gap on the perimeter. Neither 6-foot-2 guard would replicate Williams' size, though Payton plays bigger and is an elite defender in his own right. Milwaukee's Jaime Jaquez Jr. has better size but is more of an offensive force than a two-way star, and his hot start with his new team suggests the Bucks might try to re-sign him.

Ironically, the most fitting trade targets for Oklahoma City might be the two defenders who were involved in the collision that ended Williams' season: Derrick Jones Jr. and Kris Dunn. Both Clippers players are in the final seasons of their contracts, and LA needs draft picks more than their contributions to a losing cause in 2026-27. They're also excellent defenders, albeit with similar offensive question marks to Herb Jones. -- Kram

Call it now: Where will the Thunder finish in the West? The combination of Williams' loss and hot starts by the Timberwolves, Rockets and Lakers make it less likely that the Thunder will retain the West's top seed for the fourth consecutive season -- and therefore likelier that Oklahoma City and San Antonio end up on the same side of the West playoff bracket, forcing them to meet before the conference finals.

For now, I'll say that OKC tumbles to the No. 3 seed with a much less imposing defense than it's become accustomed to. An even greater downside scenario exists if more players miss significant time in the coming months. -- Kram

Oklahoma City is still is the top team in the West, even with this injury. Their 39-10 record without Williams last season proved they can still be a great team. Their bench depth -- and roster resources to help them improve -- should keep them afloat. -- Marks
